clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Case-control comparisons using linear models with covariates (age, sex, ICV, FSIQ, site); Mann-Whitney tests for comparing positive/negative deviations from normative models between ASD and controls; Pearson's correlations testing associations between clinical features (SRS-2 T-score, ADHD diagnosis, sensory alterations, RBS-R, ADOS calibrated severity score) and cerebellar structure within ASD group; support vector machine (SVM) classification with double cross-validation (10-fold outer, 5-fold inner) to predict diagnostic category; meta-analysis across sites with heterogeneity statistics (Q, I²); heterogeneity-focused analyses testing age×diagnosis, sex×diagnosis, FSIQ×diagnosis interactions using AIC model comparison; age-centered and FSIQ-centered interval analyses; matched sample analyses; dimensional analyses in HBN cohort testing SRS-2 T-score associations with linear models; sex-stratified analyses; no correction for multiple comparisons explicitly mentioned for parcellation analyses, but FDR mentioned for VBM analyses using permutation tests (10,000 permutations, voxel-wise FWE p<0.05)
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: No significant differences in cerebellar anatomy were found between individuals with autism and controls using linear models, normative modeling, or machine learning approaches; no associations between cerebellar structure and clinical features of autism were detected.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Despite comprehensive analyses using multiple methods (two parcellation pipelines, VBM, normative modeling, and machine learning), no significant case-control differences in cerebellar anatomy were identified. Linear models showed no significant effects of autism diagnosis on any cerebellar region (all p > 0.05, Cohen's f² < 0.002 for diagnosis). Normative modeling revealed no significant positive or negative deviations in cerebellar lobules when comparing ASD to controls. Support vector machine classification did not predict diagnostic category above chance level (balanced accuracy ≤ 52%). Within the ASD group, no significant correlations were found between cerebellar structure and clinical features including SRS-2 T-score, ADHD diagnosis, sensory alterations, restricted/repetitive behaviors (RBS-R), or ADOS calibrated severity score. Heterogeneity-focused analyses found no evidence of subgroup-specific cerebellar atypicalities related to sex, age, or IQ. Site-by-site meta-analysis showed only marginal uncorrected findings in 2 sites (Rome: increased lobule VI, p=0.035; Cambridge: increased crus II, p=0.048; Nijmegen: reduced vermis using SUIT, p=0.041), which were not consistent across parcellation methods. Meta-analysis heterogeneity metrics (I² ranging 0-43%) suggested no strong heterogeneity across sites. In the independent Healthy Brain Network cohort (relaxed sample n=352, stringent sample n=79 with SRS-2 T-score >76), there were no associations between autism-related symptoms (total SRS-2, SRS-2 SCI, or SRS-2 RRB subscales) and cerebellar anatomy (all p > 0.05). These negative findings held across matched samples, sex-stratified analyses, and analyses with/without FSIQ as covariate.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Concerns about validity of Short Sensory Profile psychometric properties; 3T MRI may have limitations for cerebellum due to partial volume issues (7T might detect subtle differences); possible differences in functional/structural connectivity not addressed; focus on volumetric measures only
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Concerns have been raised regarding the validity of psychometric properties of the Short Sensory Profile scale (27). While our article is focused on cerebellar volumetry using 3T MRI, this approach has limitations. The cerebellum is a highly folded structure with almost 80% of the surface area of the neocortex. Partial volume issues are thus more prominent for the cerebellum. Thus, 7T MRI (2) might be more able to detect atypicalities in cerebellar anatomy of individuals with autism. Finally, it is possible that although cerebellar anatomy appears normal using our approaches, there may still be differences in functional and structural connectivity.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Study used two different parcellation atlases (CERES and SUIT) to ensure robustness and address methodological variability in previous studies; CERES and SUIT showed moderate to strong correlation (r=0.55-0.75) but different lobule definitions (especially vermis/crus II); expert rater blinded to diagnosis performed visual QC; meta-analytic approach with site-by-site analyses to assess cross-site variability; heterogeneity-focused analyses based on Bedford et al. 2020 methodology using AIC model comparison; dimensional analyses in independent HBN cohort with both relaxed (SRS-2 T-score >60) and stringent (>76) thresholds; secondary analyses excluding FSIQ from models; matched sample analysis to address demographic differences

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is described as the largest study investigating cerebellar anatomy in autism to date. The paper explicitly addresses replicability/reproducibility issues in neuroimaging and autism research. Multiple analytical approaches were used (linear models, VBM, normative modeling, SVM, meta-analysis) to ensure robustness. The EU-AIMS LEAP cohort included 6 sites across Europe with harmonized protocols but different scanner vendors (Siemens, GE, Philips). All participants had FSIQ >70. The supplement includes extensive quality control documentation with flow charts and example images of motion artifacts and parcellation errors. 127 out of 607 total participants (20.9%) were excluded due to quality issues. Clinical measures included ADOS-2, ADI-R, SRS-2, RBS-R, SSP, and ADHD rating scale. The paper emphasizes that site-specific significant findings were inconsistent across parcellation methods and had large confidence intervals, suggesting they may represent false positives. This study represents a strong negative finding with comprehensive methodology addressing limitations of prior smaller studies.
